examples: Jesse Livermore: Limit losses immediately when a trade goes against you, treating it as the cost of doing business.
Jesse Livermore: Cut losses short and never average down on losing positions.
William O'Neil: Cut all losses immediately if a stock falls 7 to 8 percent below the purchase price without exception.
William J. O'Neil: Cut every loss quickly at around 8% to protect capital and prevent small losses from becoming catastrophic.
William O'Neil: Raise cash and refrain from buying new stocks when the general market enters a confirmed downtrend or distribution phase.
William J. O'Neil: Determine whether you are in a bull or bear market and trade in alignment with the market direction, because swimming against the current is a losing game.
Ross Haber: Market direction is crucial; most stocks follow the general market trend, so avoid trading when the market is not in an uptrend.
William O'Neil: Determine market direction using indices and increase exposure in bull markets while holding cash in bear markets.
Jesse Livermore: Treat trading as a serious business with strict rules rather than a gamble.
Jesse Livermore: Strictly follow predefined trading rules and maintain meticulous execution without letting emotions interfere.
Nicolas Darvas: The trader must remain detached and treat the market as a game of probabilities rather than a personal struggle.
Paul Tudor Jones: Focus on protecting existing capital rather than making money to survive prolonged drawdowns.
Jesse Livermore: Remove ego, hope, and outside opinions from trading to avoid disastrous psychological mistakes.
Ross Haber: Avoid letting emotions rule your trading decisions; sell down to your sleeping point if you feel anxious.
Nicolas Darvas: Remove ego from trading by acknowledging mistakes immediately and exiting losing trades fast.
Paul Tudor Jones: Treat previous trading success as irrelevant, focusing entirely on current market reality to avoid overconfidence and complacency.
Jesse Livermore: A trader must align their trades with the general market direction, only taking long positions when the overall trend is definitively upward.
Jesse Livermore: Trade in the direction of the prevailing market trend because the market is never wrong.
Jesse Livermore: Never fight the primary trend; the market is never wrong, and you must trade in the direction of prevailing momentum.
Mark Minervini: VCP works best when applied as a continuation pattern within an established existing uptrend.
William O'Neil: Establish clear rules for realizing gains and selling into strength rather than hoping for former highs.
Mark Minervini: Use trailing stop losses and scale out into strength on extended moves to lock in profits without cutting winners short prematurely.
Mark Minervini: Scale out of winning positions into strength after multiple successful natural reactions once momentum accelerates.
Nicolas Darvas: Continuously move up the stop-loss as the stock price creates new, higher Darvas boxes.
Jesse Livermore: Buy stocks that are making new highs or breaking out of sound consolidation bases rather than buying falling knives.
Jesse Livermore: Buy stocks making new highs with high volume and clear conviction rather than buying cheap stocks or trying to catch bottoms.
William O'Neil: Buy stocks as they emerge from proper consolidation bases and make new price highs rather than buying cheap or falling stocks.
William J. O'Neil: Buy stocks at new highs rather than buying cheap dips, as market winners break out to new price levels.
Jesse Livermore: The biggest money is made by sitting quietly and waiting for the right market conditions and clear leading stocks to emerge.
Jesse Livermore: Wait for pivotal points and market confirmation before entering a trade rather than acting on premature opinions.
Jesse Livermore: Wait patiently for pivotal market confirmation points rather than forcing trades or acting out of boredom.
Kristjan Kullamagi (Qullamaggie): Spend hours scanning charts every night and wait patiently for the highest-probability setups rather than forcing trades in choppy markets.
Jesse Livermore: Scale into positions incrementally, only adding to a trade when the initial stake has proven profitable.
Jesse Livermore: Scale into positions gradually, adding to winning trades rather than doubling down on losers.
Mark Minervini: Never risk more than 1 to 2 percent of your total account on any single trade.
Ed Seykota: Pyramid into winning trades by adding smaller and smaller amounts as the price moves in your favor to protect open profits.
William J. O'Neil: Concentrate on the best market leaders rather than diversifying widely across weaker stocks.
Dan Zanger: Concentrate capital into a few high-momentum leaders rather than diversifying across many mediocre stocks.
Paul Tudor Jones: Diversification across uncorrelated assets prevents total portfolio ruin when one sector or asset class experiences a major pullback.
Stanley Druckenmiller: Hold a concentrated portfolio of a few high-conviction positions rather than diversifying across dozens of mediocre ideas.
Mark Minervini: Stop-losses are placed at the low of the final contraction to maintain a favorable risk-to-reward ratio.
Kristjan Kullamagi: Place stop loss at the day's low, ensuring it is not wider than the average daily range (ADR) or true range (ATR) percentage.
Paul Tudor Jones: Limit total portfolio risk on any single trade to a small fraction, typically 1 percent or less, to survive inevitable errors.
Paul Tudor Jones: Seek a minimum risk-to-reward ratio of 5-to-1 so that you can be wrong often without losing capital.
Van Tharp: A trading system with positive expectancy combines a clear setup with sufficient opportunities to generate net profit.
Larry Williams: Rigorous quantitative testing of historical data is mandatory to validate any pattern before deploying real capital.

Jim Simons: Renaissance builds predictive mathematical models by analyzing massive historical datasets to find statistically significant pricing anomalies, prioritizing small probability edges executed at high frequency.
Cliff Asness: Academic backtests over long histories and multiple geographies confirm that buying past winners and cheap assets yields a persistent premium.
Ross Haber: Look for stocks with increasing institutional sponsorship, which provides liquidity and support.
Mark Minervini: Breakouts must be accompanied by high volume as demand outstrips supply.
Mark Minervini: Look for accumulation in the weekly volume profile showing very little or no selling pressure during pullbacks.
Nicolas Darvas: Breakouts should be accompanied by a significant increase in trading volume.
William O'Neil: Focus on companies with recent quarterly and annual earnings growth exceeding 25 percent alongside strong return on equity and new products or management.
William J. O'Neil: Look for significant recent current earnings growth and strong annual growth over the last five years.
Ross Haber: Focus on companies with at least 25% quarterly earnings growth and sales growth for at least three quarters.
Ross Haber: Look for companies with at least three years of positive annual earnings growth.
Mark Minervini: Wait for stocks in an uptrend to pull back and buy only when they turn back up rather than buying as they drop.
Kristjan Kullamaggie: After the initial strong move, wait for the stock to pull back and consolidate, building higher lows and tightening range near the rising 10 or 20 day moving average.
Ross Cameron: A micro-pullback (a short pause in a strong trend) is a valid entry point for momentum trades.
Andrew Aziz: Buy strong momentum stocks when they pull back to the 20 EMA on a 2-minute chart (the 9/20 strategy).
